Work

How I Think About Stakeholder Management

By Furaihan Kamyl Arnazaye · 2026 · 4 min read
In short
  • At the desk, the work is understanding the issue, mapping stakeholders as institutions and as people, then building the narrative and choosing the channel.
  • Beyond the desk, it is relationships built over time, public communication on a parallel track, and coalitions when a position carries more weight together.
  • My own experience sits mostly on the desk side. I would rather be precise about that than blur it.

Most of what determines whether a policy conversation goes well happens before anyone enters the room.

By the time a meeting starts, the real work has usually already been done. Understanding the issue, mapping who matters and why, deciding what to say and how to say it. What happens in the room is often just the execution of a plan built at a desk.

I find it useful to think about this work through a framework from Young and Quinn (2012), which breaks advocacy into three components: a way into the process, the message and the activities built around it, and the messenger delivering it. It maps closely onto how policy communication actually works, and it gives me a way to describe the discipline without making it sound more mysterious than it is.

At the Desk

Every issue starts with understanding it properly. Not just the surface position, but the regulatory mechanics, the competing interests, and where the genuine points of friction sit. This is the unglamorous part. Reading, cross-referencing, and building a mental model of the issue that is accurate rather than convenient.

From there the work moves to mapping stakeholders at both the institutional and the individual level. An institution has a position. The people inside it have histories, incentives, and relationships that shape how that position gets expressed and how much room there is to engage with it. A ministry's official stance and the way a specific director general has historically approached similar issues are not always the same thing. Treating them as identical is a common mistake. Part of that mapping is understanding how a stakeholder has positioned itself on related issues over time, including the pattern behind it. It is less about tracking any single statement and more about building a coherent sense of where an institution has consistently stood, where it has shifted, and why.

Once the issue and the stakeholders are understood, the communication strategy follows. What the core narrative should be, which framing will land with which audience, and which channel makes sense for which message. A formal media statement carries different weight than a direct conversation, and choosing wrong undermines all the work that came before it. The issue understanding, the stakeholder map, and the narrative become the capital you carry into every conversation that follows. None of it stays at the desk.

Beyond the Desk

The other half of the work happens away from it, because preparation only matters if it translates into real engagement, and engagement happens through relationships. Formal and informal, built deliberately over time rather than assembled the moment they are needed.

This starts before any direct contact exists. Knowing who to reach out to, through which channel, with what framing, is itself a skill. It continues through the first meeting, where the goal is rarely to resolve anything immediately. Then it extends into the long, less visible work of maintaining a relationship across both professional and casual contexts, because trust built only in formal settings tends to be thinner than trust built across both.

Public communication runs on a parallel track. Media coverage shapes how an institution's position is understood by audiences who will never sit in a meeting but whose perception still matters. Knowing when to communicate through media rather than through direct channels, and keeping those two tracks coherent, is part of the same discipline. At a wider scale, the work sometimes involves building coalitions with industry peers around shared issues. Some positions carry more weight collectively than individually, and alignment with other actors facing the same regulatory questions can shift how an issue is received.

I should be honest about where my own experience sits within that second half. Most of my work has concentrated on the desk side of the framework. Issue analysis, stakeholder mapping, and communication strategy, along with the public-facing dimensions of engagement. I have had much less direct exposure to the relational, in-person dimension of advocacy, the kind of personal relationship cultivated over years of informal contact.

I have studied that dimension closely, because understanding how it works is part of understanding the whole system. Claiming expertise in something you have only observed is different from being clear about what you have done versus what you understand conceptually. I would rather be precise about that line than blur it.

Advocacy is a system. The issue you understand, the stakeholders you have mapped, the message you have built, the relationships you maintain, and the channels you choose.

The room matters. But it is the smallest part of the work.
